citation: Kholodov A; Graham D; Moon W (2018): Soil Physical, Chemical, and Thermal Characterization, Council Road Site, Seward Peninsula, Alaska, 2016. Next-Generation Ecosystem Experiments (NGEE) Arctic. Dataset. doi:10.5440/1417652

dataset.name: Soil Physical, Chemical, and Thermal Characterization, Council Road Site, Seward Peninsula, Alaska, 2016
description: This dataset provides the results of physical, chemical, and thermal characterization of soils at the Council Road Site, Seward Peninsula, Alaska. Soil pits were dug from 11 September 2016 at three locations CPIT1, CPIT3, and CPIT4 at the Council Road MM71 Site (CN_MM71). This dataset includes field observations and descriptions of soil layers or horizons, field measurements of soil volumetric water content, soil temperature, thermal conductivity, and heat capacity. Laboratory measurements (*.csv files) of soil properties include gravimetric water content, bulk density, volumetric water content, and total carbon and nitrogen. A synthesis data file (*.csv), photographs (*.jpg) of the respective soil pits, and a user guide (*.pdf) are also included.

The Next-Generation Ecosystem Experiments: Arctic (NGEE Arctic), was a research effort to reduce uncertainty in Earth System Models by developing a predictive understanding of carbon-rich Arctic ecosystems and feedbacks to climate. NGEE Arctic was supported by the Department of Energy's Office of Biological and Environmental Research. The NGEE Arctic project had two field research sites: 1) located within the Arctic polygonal tundra coastal region on the Barrow Environmental Observatory (BEO) and the North Slope near Utqiagvik (Barrow), Alaska and 2) multiple areas on the discontinuous permafrost region of the Seward Peninsula north of Nome, Alaska. Through observations, experiments, and synthesis with existing datasets, NGEE Arctic provided an enhanced knowledge base for multi-scale modeling and contributed to improved process representation at global pan-Arctic scales within the Department of Energy's Earth system Model (the Energy Exascale Earth System Model, or E3SM), and specifically within the E3SM Land Model component (ELM).

measurementTechnique:
Thaw Depth:
Tile probe depth was measured by inserting a 48-inch long fiberglass tile probe with 5/8-inch steel tip into the soil manually. A value of 100 cm (Flag V2) indicates the probe was fully inserted and did not reach permafrost or rock.

Volumetric Water Content:
Volumetric water content was measured using a 5TE soil moisture sensor (Decagon Devices) with mineral or organic calibrations and a ProCheck meter. For organic soils, the maximum measurable dielectric permittivity is ~30, therefore higher values are represented by the maximum VWC (0.86 m³/m³). Temperature was measured using a HH502 Digital Thermometer (Omega) with a type K thermocouple, stainless steel sheath, and ice-point calibration. Depth includes height of nearby vegetation.

Soil Samples:
Soil samples were removed from the face of soil pits in a 2-inch ring using an AMS sampler. Soil samples were weighed in the laboratory, and two subsamples were dried at 100 degC to determine the average gravimetric water content. Bulk density values were calculated by dividing the extrapolated dry weight of the soil sample by the original 90 cm3 sample volume. The volumetric water content (θv) was calculated by multiplying the gravimetric water content by the bulk density.

Gravimetric Water Content:
Gravimetric water content (g H2O g-1 dwt. soil). Gravimetric water content: Approximately 5 g wet soil was placed in a pre-weighed tin. Soils were dried at 101°C to constant mass (up to 24 hours).

XRF Spectroscopy:
Energy Dispersive X-ray Fluorescence (XRF) spectroscopy was used to estimate concentrations of major elements and trace elements. Measurements were made on dried, ground, homogenized samples using a Bruker XRF Tracer III-SD handheld XRF, under vacuum with no filter, at 15 kV/25microA. Concentrations are normalized by the highest TiO2 amounts in the soil series sample, and are also normalized to account for C and N in the sample. Major elements are shown in oxide form (as weight percent). Trace elements are shown in elemental form (mg/Kg). Both are normalized as described above. Measurements below the limit of detection are shown as 0.
